newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to discuss revoking more Burmese trade perks.
newsitem.headline: EU to discuss revoking more Burmese trade perks.

text.p: The European Union may decide as early as Monday to withdraw special trading privileges from Burma's agricultural products because of growing unease over its human rights record, diplomatic sources said on Tuesday.

They said EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels next week will discuss a European Commission proposal made on Tuesday to strip Burma of Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) trade benefits on agricultural products.
The Commission said in a statement it would ask the foreign ministers to revoke Burma's GSP following an investigation into Burmese labour practices.
Foreign ministers were originally due to discuss the subject on March 24, but diplomatic sources said this was now likely to be brought forward.
In London, Human Rights watch, which has long campaigned for further isolation of Burma, said it welcomed the move.
"We are extremely pleased with this move," said a spokeswoman, "but we are are looking for still more leverage from the international community."
The Commission investigation follows complaints from international and European non-governmental groups that Burma was using forced and child labour to boost its exports.
The Commission said Burma refused to cooperate with the investigation.
In December, the European Commission scrapped Burma's industrial GSP privileges for the same reason.
EU-Burma trade totals around 41 million European currency units a year with around a quarter subject to GSP benefits which include lucrative tax and tarioff breaks.

The latest move comes less than a week after EU foreign ministers agonised with their Association of Southeast Asian Nations counterparts over the best way to bring Burma back into the international community.
The EU, which favours isolating Rangoon, was warned by ASEAN ministers that it had no say in whether Burma would be made a member of the Asian group.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, who will be at Monday's EU meeting, said in Singapore that Burma was "a nasty, repressive regime".

The Commission stance is not likely to please Asian leaders who appeared to be trying to persuade Europe to coax Burma's pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi into dropping her call for sanctions against Rangoon.
Suu Kyi has called repeatedly for sanctions against Burma's State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), which seized power in 1988 and ignored the results of subsequent elections her party won.

Doug Bereuter, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives sub-committee on East Asia and the Pacific, said on Friday that stepped-up repression in Burma required President Bill Clinton to ban new U.S. investment there.
